In 2026, the Kitchener Indoor Recreation Complex, or Kirk, will be one of the premier indoor
recreation facilities in Kitchener and one of the best indoor turf facilities in all
of Ontario.
The facility is expected to attract more than 570,000 visits annually, including an estimated
100,000 event-related visits from out-of-town coaches, event officials and spectators.
Not only will Kirk be the City's first-ever net-zero building, it will also be the City's
most accessible building.
As a reminder, Kirk is being built as a multi-sport venue that will meet the growing and increasingly
diverse recreation needs of our community, while also attracting major tournaments and
other sporting events that will benefit many local businesses.
The facility itself will include a FIFA-sized indoor turf that will be divisible into four
fields, a world-class aquatic centre with two pools, a quad gymnasium, two cricket practice
nets, an elevated walking track and several multi-purpose rooms.
Today we're excited to share with Council an operating model, including a staffing model
and operating budget that supports the operation of the Kirk as Kitchener's premier indoor
recreation destination by ensuring a great customer experience for residents and visitors
alike.
Before I get into the details of the proposed operating model, it is important to stress
that the operating model before you today for your consideration will have no direct
impact on existing taxpayers as the costs of operating the facility will be funded through
fees paid by facility users themselves and by anticipated assessment growth.
Designed using staff interviews, local comparators and detailed facility usage projections, the
Kirk staffing model reflects the City's commitment to customer service in many ways.
It provides for the facility to be open to the public from 7 a.m. to midnight, seven
days a week.
It also allows for the proactive provision of a great customer experience, including
the maintenance and cleanliness of the facility, its amenities and equipment, as well as the
flexibility to increase staffing levels as required to support the busiest times at the
facility, all while ensuring that residents and visitors feel welcomed.
In addition, the proposed staffing model ensures there will be expertise in planning and supporting
multiple major tournaments and events each year, all of which will bring thousands of
visitors to the facility and support local businesses.
And I'm happy to report that the proposed staffing model will allow the City to offer
more youth drop-in opportunities and 200 additional weekly spots in our highly sought-after March
break and summer camps.
As part of the City's Sport Division, the Kirk team will include three teams working
together to fulfil the City's commitment to creating a positive customer experience
for visitors.
The aquatics team will provide aquatic programming, including meets and events, and oversee daily
pool operations.
The customer experience team will ensure seamless access to programs and amenities, and a well
maintained facility and provide frontline customer service.
And the events and booking team will ensure the facility is fully utilized through rentals,
programs, events and tournaments.
This Kirk staff team will be supported by subject matter experts from other areas of
the organization such as facilities management who will lend their expertise to help run
the facility.
The Kirk leadership team includes a facility manager and a supervisor of each of the three
teams.
Recruitment of the management team will begin shortly with the aim of having them on board
by the end of this year so that they are able to hire, onboard and train their staff as
well as complete the operational planning and programming work needed before the facility
opens later in 2026.

Good afternoon, Mayor Vrbanovic and members of Council.
As mentioned, my name is Bethany Pierce and I supervise older adult services.
In my role, I connect with Kitchener's older adult population on a daily basis and I really
get to see firsthand just how our programs and services positively impact the lives of
so many of our residents.
Today staff are seeking direction on the next phase of the Rockaway redevelopment which
will have a significant impact on the future of older adult programming.
The redevelopment of Rockaway Centre has been discussed for many years.
Council provided previous direction in 2010, 2013 and 2019 to pursue a partnership with
a private sector to redevelop Rockaway Centre into a medium to high density residential
building that includes a ground floor older adult community centre as well as possible ancillary,
medical, dental, retail and office type uses. In April 2024, Council approved a three-phase plan
to redevelop Rockway Centre. Both phase one and two are complete. Staff are ready to move to phase
three which brings us to today's discussion. In 2024, staff led a community engagement process
to better understand the atmosphere, site features and program offerings residents would
like to see in a new older adult centre. I will share a high-level overview of the engagement
results before outlining the details of the next phase of the project. Our engagement tactics
included online surveys, in-person conversations, site visits and events like Rockin and Rockway,
which we saw so many of you attend. Based on the engagement results, we learned the top features
are a cafe or a coffee shop, fitness room, outdoor spaces, on-site parking, drop-off and pickup zone.
We also heard that 60% of the respondents want space for socializing or casual interactions.
Overall, 50% thought that they would like an outdoor space of some kind and find it very
valuable. Accessibility, affordability and safety were key themes that emerged in the consultation.
Residents also expressed that they would like a wide range of programs and services. The older
adult population that is looking for active recreation and they're also looking for things
like cards and games, arts and crafts and health and wellness workshops.
Based on the input collected through user group and community engagement, as well as subject
matter expertise, staff developed a list of deliverables for a new older adult centre.
This list strongly reflects the community input collected through the public engagement process.
Taken together, these deliverables would result in a centre that is approximately 8,200 square
feet larger than the existing Rockway Centre. It would also feature 800 additional square
feet of outdoor space and 50 additional parking spaces than our current facility. This would
be the City's largest community centre.
Based on the results of community engagement, staff are recommending that the following
requirements be included in a new older adult centre. 21,000 to 26,000 square feet, 1,200
1,600 square feet of outdoor space, a minimum of 150 on-site surface parking spaces, a drop-off
and pickup zone near the entrance of the building, close to the LRT and or bus routes, a double
sport gymnasium, a multi-purpose fitness room with appropriate sport flooring, a large space for
creative art programming like pottery and painting, a billiards room, one large and
one medium multipurpose room for programs, meetings and events, a warming kitchen, large
lobby space with cafe and lots of comfortable and accessible seating.
We will have staff workspaces and a welcoming service counter.
and universal washrooms, the whole building will be fully accessible and will be built
to higher accessibility standard than what provincial legislation dictates.
In addition to the list of deliverables, staff are also seeking direction from Council to
explore an alternative location for the new Older Adult Centre.
The existing site has not been ruled out.
However, there are many reasons why the City should consider alternate locations within
a 1.5-kilometre radius of the existing site. First, by building at another location, we
can keep the existing facility open and minimize program disruptions. If construction on the
existing site is required, it will cause significant disruption and inconvenience to Rockway users
and potentially a facility closure during the construction period, which can last for
several years. Second, the City can likely build something
faster on an alternate site. By partnering with a developer that already owns property
and is ready to build, we can more likely build a new facility faster than we would
if we stay on the existing site. And last, by going to an alternate location,
it provides the city with an opportunity to sell the existing Rockway site and reinvest
those funds into the development of a new facility. Ten years ago, City Council allocated
$6 million into the capital budget. With rising inflation and construction costs, there will
be a significant gap in the funding required versus the funding available for this project.
Again, there is no final decision about the location of the new older adult facility.
Staff are asking Council to consider proposals from developers within 1.5 kilometres of the
existing site including the current Rockway Centre for this mixed-use project. That concludes
the presentation and we're happy to take any questions.
